e.t: “Angia” is a personal name, also rendered “Anggia,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 6:15. Because it functions as a proper name and no verse text is supplied here, its significance cannot be explained beyond identifying the person named in that genealogy. The spelling may appear slightly different in English, but the lexical identity remains the same.

This Greek LXX noun means “crime”: a wrongful act or offense that brings guilt. It refers to conduct judged to be seriously wrong, whether against another person, the community, or what God requires. The word appears 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in this corpus, including passages about accusations, confessed wrongdoing, and the removal of guilt. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains an actual offense or unlawful deed.

This Greek LXX verb means “gather round”: to bring people together or assemble them in one place. It describes the act of collecting a group, whether people are called together or brought together by circumstances. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, showing a repeated sense of assembling rather than merely being present. Its exact force in any verse depends on who is gathered and why.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Aidan; Ethan.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 23:9. Since it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: distinguishing the individual who bears the name. The exact person and significance of the name in that passage require the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “governor of the citadel” or a “guardian”—someone responsible for protecting and overseeing a fortified place. The word can therefore describe a person who holds authority over a citadel while also carrying the duty of guarding it. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 3:13. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a citadel’s appointed protector or governor.

“One another” refers to people or things considered mutually or reciprocally, connecting one member with the others in a group. It is a pronoun, so it points back to persons or things already understood from the surrounding sentence rather than naming them. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs 40 times, showing a repeated way of expressing mutual relationships or actions. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding words and context.

Amital is a proper name—the personal name Amital. It functions as a name rather than as a description, action, or general religious term. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears three times, in two books: twice in 2 Kings and once in 2 Chronicles. The available wording consistently presents it as “Amital,” so no broader meaning should be attached to it here without additional scriptural context. Its occurrences are found at 2 Kings 23:31, 2 Kings 24:18, and 2 Chronicles 36:2.

This verb means “run back”: it describes moving back toward a previous place or point. As a verb, it expresses the action itself rather than a person or object. In this Greek biblical corpus, it appears only twice, both in 2 Maccabees, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The exact force—such as urgency, distance, or purpose—must be determined from each passage’s context.

This verb means “speak against; answer.” It describes a spoken response that may oppose what another person has said, or may simply answer that person. Its basic function is to mark speech directed back toward someone, especially when disagreement or a reply is involved. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:1. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means obstinacy: a stubborn refusal to yield or change course. It describes a settled resistance rather than a momentary hesitation, though the precise force in any sentence depends on its surrounding context. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. The word therefore names a quality of persistent stubbornness, not an action or person. Its central idea is resistance that remains firm when obedience, persuasion, or correction would call for a different response.

This Greek LXX verb means “put out” or “extinguish.” It describes stopping something that is burning, shining, or otherwise giving off heat or light. As an action word, it focuses on causing that activity to cease rather than merely becoming weaker. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including Proverbs, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “bravely.” As an adverb, it describes an action carried out with courage and boldness, telling how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: the action is performed courageously rather than timidly or fearfully.

Asgad is a proper name, rendered “Asgad” or “Azgath.” It identifies a named individual or family designation in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs four times in the LXX corpus, in Ezra and Nehemiah, including lists associated with the returned community. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific person or family connection cannot be stated more precisely. Its basic meaning is therefore the name itself: Asgad, also rendered Azgath.

This adjective describes something lewd—sexually improper, indecent, or morally unrestrained. It characterizes conduct or speech that violates proper sexual modesty rather than expressing a neutral description. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, the word occurs only once, in Sirach 23:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is clear: it identifies behavior or expression as lewd and improper.

Achikam is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name is rendered “Achikam” and is preserved as a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs 10 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, across Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah. The supplied references identify places where this person’s name appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each individual role or event.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Baithēra” or “Vethira.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, both occurrences being in Judges 7:24. Its exact referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a name, not as a common noun with a broader descriptive meaning.

Beelmeōn is a proper name referring to a place, rendered as “Beelmeōn” or “Veelmeon.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Numbers 32:38. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific historical or contextual significance cannot be stated here; its basic function is to identify the place named Beelmeōn.

Berea, also called Verea, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this word appears once, in 1 Maccabees 9:4. The name itself identifies the location rather than describing an action, quality, person, or spiritual concept. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s specific role in that sentence cannot be explained further. Its basic meaning is simply the place-name Berea.

Bosor, also rendered Vosor, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place in the Greek Old Testament and related books. The name appears 12 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Deuteronomy, Joshua, and 1 Samuel. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and setting, but its basic function is geographical identification.

Gaam is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 22:24. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who someone is called, not what that person does or represents. The name’s specific significance in Genesis 22:24 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective means “calm,” describing someone or something marked by quietness rather than agitation or disturbance. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a peaceful or settled condition. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:6. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be described further; its ordinary meaning remains a calm or tranquil state.

This adjective means “sweet,” describing a taste that is sugary or pleasing to the palate. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 15 times, showing that it is a recurring word for sweetness rather than a rare expression. Its exact force—whether describing food, drink, or another comparison—depends on the sentence where it appears, but its central meaning remains the same: something sweet in taste.

Goliath is a proper name referring to the Philistine warrior known by that name in the Greek Old Testament and in Sirach. It is not a general word describing a quality or action, but a personal designation. The name occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: four times in the Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its uses refer to the same named biblical figure or to a person identified by that name, while the surrounding verse determines the particular event being mentioned.

This word means “lender,” a person who provides money or other resources to someone with the expectation of repayment. As a noun, it identifies the one who gives a loan rather than the borrower who receives it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, showing a focused reference to the person involved in lending. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its teaching about debt, obligation, or repayment.

This Greek verb describes being “in straits” or coming to “take offense.” It can express a person’s difficult or pressured condition, or the reaction of taking offense. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central sense concerns distress or offense.

This noun means “attendance” or “service”—being present to help, care for, or carry out a duty. It describes an act of serving rather than a person who serves. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:58. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact force in that passage must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains practical service or attendance given to others.

This verb means “cross over”: to move from one side of a place or boundary to the other. It describes passage across something, whether a physical route, region, or barrier. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, with most occurrences in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being crossed and the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains movement from one side to another.

This verb means “narrate” or “describe”: to tell something in an orderly or understandable way. It can refer to recounting events, reporting what has happened, or putting an experience into words for someone else. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 64 times, showing a broad use for communicating experiences, reports, and accounts. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on what is being recounted and to whom it is told.

This adjective describes something made in a net-like or latticed pattern. It can refer to an object or surface formed with an open, interwoven structure rather than a solid, continuous one. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs four times, describing such construction or design. Its central idea is not a net as an object, but the quality of being “made in net fashion” or “latticed.”

“Dorkōn” or “Thorkon” is a proper name, identifying a person or named figure rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Song of Songs 2:17. The available information establishes the name itself, but not the person’s identity or significance apart from that passage. Its precise reference in the verse therefore depends on the surrounding text and context.

This Greek LXX proper noun is a personal name, rendered “Dōra” or “Thora.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. The name occurs 73 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, across 69 verses. Its exact reference may identify different individuals, so the surrounding verse is needed to determine whom it names in a particular passage.

Ezer is a personal name, preserved as a name rather than translated into a descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in 1 Chronicles 7:21 and once in Ezekiel 11:1. Because the available information identifies it only as Ezer, its central meaning is the name itself, while the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person bears it in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “cancel; set aside.” It describes an action that removes something from effect or places it to one side rather than allowing it to stand or continue. As a verb, it expresses what someone does, not a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 7:14. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is to cancel something or set it aside.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an “elephant” or to “ivory,” naming either the animal itself or the valuable material associated with it. Its exact sense is determined by how the sentence uses the word. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 6:46. No broader usage pattern is available from additional occurrences, so the central meaning remains the straightforward identification of an elephant or ivory.

This Greek LXX verb means “leap out of” or “leap up.” It describes a sudden jumping movement away from a place or upward from it. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nahum 3:17. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from that context; but its basic action is a quick, energetic leap or springing movement.

This LXX verb means “sound out”: to make something heard or announce it aloud. It describes the act of giving a sound public expression rather than keeping it silent. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Joel, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains vocalizing or broadcasting something so that it can be heard.

This adjective means “towards the right,” describing a direction or position on the right side. It identifies where something is oriented or located rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 34:16. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains directional: movement or orientation toward the right. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament corpus.

This adjective means “expert”: someone recognized as having knowledge or skill. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes a person whose understanding makes him fit to advise, judge, or carry out a task wisely. The word occurs 11 times, including passages in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Daniel, and Sirach. Its emphasis is not merely on possessing information, but on being knowledgeable and capable in a practical sense.

This verb means “shine on”: it describes light giving brightness or falling upon something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Job, so its basic sense is focused rather than broad or varied. The word may be used for light that visibly shines, while the surrounding verse determines what is being illuminated. Its central idea remains the active presence or effect of shining. citep03:word:lxx:L705321:identity citep03:word:lxx:L705321:occurrences

This verb means to “stir up” or “excite,” describing an action that awakens, encourages, or intensifies a response. It focuses on moving someone or something toward stronger activity or feeling rather than simply naming a state. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the deliberate stirring or rousing of a response.

This Greek LXX word means “yet” or “still,” indicating that something continues, remains, or is true up to a particular point. As an adverb or conjunction, it can connect an ongoing condition with what follows, often marking continuation in time or circumstance. It occurs 496 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a common word for expressing that something has not ended or changed. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Ephod is the name of an ephod, a noun referring to a particular biblical item. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears four times, all in Judges, from Judges 17:5 through Judges 18:20. Its lexical meaning is simply “ephod,” without a fuller description of the item’s purpose or significance. That specific force must be understood from the surrounding passage in each verse.

Zabdias is a proper name, also rendered Zavthias. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears three times, in three verses: once in 1 Chronicles and twice in 2 Chronicles. The name itself does not provide further meaning about the individuals who bear it; their identity and role must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This word describes strong, ardent feeling expressed as zeal or jealousy. As a noun, it can refer to passionate devotion, earnest concern, or an intense desire that another person or cause receive what is due. Its meaning may be favorable or unfavorable depending on the surrounding passage: zeal stresses fervent commitment, while jealousy stresses protective or possessive intensity. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 39 times, showing a recurring word for powerful emotional commitment rather than a mild interest.

Thaanach is a proper name, also given as “Thaanakh.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Kings 4:12 and 1 Chronicles 7:29. Those references establish where the name appears, while the name’s precise referent in each passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means pressure. It describes a condition in which someone is pressed, constrained, or placed under difficult force. The word occurs 129 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a recurring term for hardship or oppressive circumstances rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “17,” functioning as a number rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Psalm 118:129. Its role is simply to identify the number seventeen; the precise significance of that number in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus, not treated as a Greek New Testament word.

Iōrib, also given as “Ioriv,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah 11—once in verse 5 and once in verse 10. The available information identifies the term as a name but does not provide a further lexical definition or the verse text needed to explain its particular role in either passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as “working perversely” or “working evil.” It portrays action as deliberately corrupt or harmful rather than merely difficult or unsuccessful. As an adjective, it characterizes a person, activity, or work according to its evil manner or purpose. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:8; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “made of flax,” describing something produced from the fibers of the flax plant. It is a noun referring to a flax-made material or object, rather than expressing an action or quality in the abstract. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 1:6. Its basic sense identifies the substance from which something is made; the surrounding verse determines the particular item being described.

This verb means “tyrannize”: to exercise harsh, oppressive power over others. It describes domination that is forceful rather than gentle or just, focusing on what a person does to those under his control. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 33 times, including passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains oppressive rule or treatment.

gl: remind oneself of sth; call to mind sth
d: remind oneself of sth; call to mind sth

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to remind oneself of something or to call something to mind. It describes the act of bringing a person, matter, or thought back into one’s own remembrance. The wording is reflexive in sense: the person doing the remembering turns the thought back toward himself or herself. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 13:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is deliberate recollection.

This Greek LXX verb means “take note of”: to notice something and give it attentive consideration. It describes an active response rather than merely having something present in view. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, showing a repeated call to recognize or attend to what is being observed. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains deliberate attention to something noticed.

This noun means “settlement”: a place where people dwell or are established. It refers to an inhabited place rather than to the act of settling itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 19 times, including passages concerning God’s dwelling place and the places where people live. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a settled habitation or dwelling place. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

Kedel, also rendered Kethel, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or name-bearing figure in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezra 2:47. The available information establishes the name’s form and use as a personal designation, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the individual or the significance of the name.

“Key” refers to an object used to open or secure a lock. As a noun, the word names the physical instrument itself rather than the act of opening. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs four times, including references in Judges, 1 Chronicles, Job, and Bel and the Dragon. The exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a key.

This word means “glue,” a substance used to join things so they hold together. It is a noun, naming the material itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 44:13. The word’s precise role there depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning remains glue: a joining material used to attach one thing to another.

This Greek LXX noun means “precipice,” referring to the edge or steep face of a high drop. It names a physical feature of the land rather than an action, emotion, or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within one verse in 2 Chronicles 25:12. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but the word itself points plainly to a steep, dangerous descent or cliff edge.

This verb means “make to rattle”—to cause a sound or movement marked by repeated knocking, shaking, or clattering. It describes an action rather than an object, so the surrounding sentence identifies what is being made to rattle. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 11 verses, showing that it is used in several settings while retaining this basic sense. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

This adjective describes something stained or polluted with bloodshed, emphasizing defilement by gore. It presents a condition marked by violent blood contamination rather than ordinary dirt or impurity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Wisdom 11:6, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains clear: something made foul, polluted, or ceremonially unclean through contact with gore.

Masphassat is a proper name, rendered “Masphassat” and also identified as “Masfassat.” It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 19:29. Because it is a name rather than a common noun, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular person or place in the biblical record, not a general quality or action. The available wording does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or explain the name’s origin.

Messara is a proper name, preserved in the Greek Old Testament as “Messara.” As a name, it identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing a general quality or action. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Samuel—at 1 Samuel 23:19 and 1 Samuel 24:23. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its basic function is clear: Messara is a distinctive name used to identify something or someone.

This Greek LXX verb means “devise” or “construct”: it describes the act of planning or making something. It presents purposeful human activity rather than a mere accident or occurrence. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 2 Chronicles 26:15. Without the verse text, its precise reference in that sentence cannot be expanded further, but its central meaning remains the deliberate devising or construction of something.

This proper name refers to the Minaioi, also called the Minei. It identifies a particular people or group rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs four times: twice in 2 Chronicles and twice in Job. The supplied lexical meaning gives the group’s name, while the individual passages provide the context for how that name functions there.

Miphithim is a proper name, referring to a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 2:53, and is rendered “Miphithim.” The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning. Its precise reference must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the name alone.

Mosollam is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears nine times across nine verses, in genealogical and historical passages. Because it is a name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it distinguishes one individual from others who are mentioned. The name occurs in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Nehemiah, but the references provided do not include the surrounding verse text needed to describe each person or explain the role any one Mosollam played.

This noun refers to a quarrel or wrangle—a verbal dispute marked by contention between people. It names the conflict itself rather than describing a person who argues. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 13 times, showing a recurring word for strife in wisdom, prophetic, and lament passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains an argument or contentious dispute.

This noun means a “small spit,” referring to a slender pointed implement. It names a concrete object rather than an action, quality, or person. In this LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Job and once in 4 Maccabees. The references are Job 41:22 and 4 Maccabees 11:19, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use in either passage.

This adjective means “looking backwards.” It describes something oriented toward what is behind rather than what is ahead. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 9:23, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word itself gives a clear visual idea: turning or directing one’s gaze toward the rear. It is a description of direction or posture, not a broad abstract term.

This noun means “guard hut; lodge,” referring to a small place where someone stays or keeps watch. It is a concrete term for a simple shelter rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Psalms, Isaiah, and Micah. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “trap”: to catch or ensnare someone through a snare, scheme, or other means that prevents escape. It describes an action rather than the trap itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Samuel 28:9 and Ecclesiastes 9:12. The surrounding verse determines whether the trapping is presented as a deliberate act by people or as a broader picture of how someone may unexpectedly be caught.

“Highest of all” describes something placed above every other thing in rank, position, or degree. It is an adjective expressing the strongest possible comparison, not merely something high. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 1:20; the reference identifies its only occurrence, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine what it describes there. Its central sense is being above all others in the comparison.

This verb means to “stretch out in line,” describing something extended so that it runs along an ordered line or row. It focuses on lengthening or laying something out in sequence, rather than simply moving or reaching. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in Ezekiel. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb describes something embroidered or decorated around its edge. It refers to adding stitched ornament along the outer border of an object, rather than simply making the object itself. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 36:13, and its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse text. Its central idea is edging a material with embroidery or decorative stitching.

περιφορά refers to “meats carried round”—food being carried or circulated. As a noun, it names this thing or activity rather than describing a person or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Ecclesiastes, so its recorded use is narrow and concrete. The surrounding verse determines how this idea functions in each occurrence, but the central sense remains something carried around for distribution or presentation.

This verb means “enrich”: to make something richer, fuller, or more productive. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for increasing the abundance or fruitful condition of something. It occurs eight times in the LXX corpus, including passages from Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being enriched and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun refers to prostration—the condition or act of lying prostrate, with the body lowered down. It describes someone physically cast down or lying flat rather than standing. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX material represented here, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains bodily prostration or lying prostrate.

This adjective means “like fire” or “fiery.” It describes something by comparing its character or appearance to fire, whether in brightness, heat, intensity, or a similar quality; the exact force depends on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 43:4. Its basic sense is vivid and energetic, presenting fire as the comparison that helps describe the person or thing in view.

This Greek LXX noun means “small pomegranate” or “pomegranate shape.” It refers either to the small fruit itself or to an object made in that form. In the Old Testament Greek, it is used especially in descriptions of ornamental designs and furnishings connected with the tabernacle and temple. The word occurs nine times in the LXX corpus, with most occurrences in Exodus and Chronicles. Its precise reference in any particular passage depends on the surrounding description.

Saboud, also rendered Savuth, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament, and it appears only once in this corpus, in 1 Chronicles 4:26. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its identity is clear while the person’s role and significance must be understood from that passage.

This is a proper name, rendered “Salōmōn” or “Salomon,” referring to a person rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Proverbs: once at Proverbs 1:1 and once at Proverbs 32:1. The name itself identifies the person; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain what is being said about him in either reference.

This noun means “Seraphs,” referring to beings identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs twice, both times in Isaiah 6, at Isaiah 6:2 and Isaiah 6:6. The word itself supplies the group’s designation, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain what the seraphs are doing or what their presence means in each passage. Its usage is therefore specific and limited within the LXX corpus.
